variant_reviews.comparison: For each positive time i, a finite I within {1,...,i}, and any possibly infinite future J, require rejection of I to imply rejection of I union J. This does not permit inserting omitted past indices and is weaker than monotonicity under arbitrary supersets. Standard process predictability does not express this property. The source generally interprets comparisons almost surely under each model law; separate comparisons over uncountably many subsets cannot silently be promoted to one common full-measure event needed for pointwise finite-prefix reduction.

variant_reviews.comparison: For each rejected I there must be an i in I such that every J subset of I containing i is rejected. The witness may depend on both I and the outcome, and J is not restricted to finite subsets. This is neither arbitrary-superset rejection nor merely rejection of some singleton. The empty-intersection test is fixed to zero in the source, so no empty-set witness is demanded. Preserve the source's almost-sure convention and its unresolved uncountable-family simultaneity rather than inferring a measurable witness or stronger pointwise property.

variant_reviews.comparison: For fixed model law P, the event of any false rejection is the countable union over j with P in H_j of {d_j=1}; finite-prefix events increase to it. The inspected continuity theorem gives convergence of their extended measures, and for probability laws conversion to real probabilities is finite. Strong control quantifies over all P, not only the global null. The cumulative count may be infinite, so use an extended count or the equivalent event rather than a real limit assumed finite. Adapted binary decisions make the countable error event measurable; the library theorem's allowance for nonmeasurable sets does not resolve the paper's separate arbitrary uncountable-closure measurability issue.
